node.description: A historian of the American West, of Native American history and of environmental history. The Middle Ground (1991; quoted from Cambridge Core first-page excerpts of the introduction and chapters) rejects accounts of Indian–white contact with 'but two outcomes', conquest or persistence, because contact 'creates as well as destroys': in the Great Lakes pays d'en haut, French and Algonquian allies 'had to arrive at some common conception of suitable ways of acting', a middle ground which White describes as a process of creative and often expedient misunderstanding, sustained because whites could not simply command Indians or disregard them, until in the nineteenth century its compromises 'yielded to stark choices between assimilation and otherness'. His environmental books trace Salish and settler land use and environmental change in Island County, Washington (1980), subsistence, environment and dependency among the Choctaws, Pawnees and Navajos (1983), and the Columbia River as an organic machine, an energy system remade by human labour that keeps natural qualities, in which human work is energy as much as the river's flow (1995). His 1985 Pacific Historical Review essay surveyed environmental history as a new field, and he responded to Worster's agroecological essay in the 1990 Journal of American History round table. His later work also addresses memory, capitalism and American national history. Remembering Ahanagran (1998; 2003 paperback) examines family recollection against historical evidence, according to its publisher’s account. The companion description of Railroaded (2011) connects railway corporations, debt, political patronage, economic instability and western landscapes; the book itself is not read here. His 2010 working paper treats collaborative digital visualization as a method of historical research. The later selection includes The Republic for Which It Stands (2017), California Exposures (documented in 2020, with photographs by Jesse Amble White) and Who Killed Jane Stanford? (2022).
node.representative_figures_and_works: Richard White (b. 1947); Land Use, Environment, and Social Change: The Shaping of Island County, Washington (1980; 1992 paperback with Cronon's foreword and a new preface); The Roots of Dependency: Subsistence, Environment, and Social Change among the Choctaws, Pawnees, and Navajos (1983); “American Environmental History: The Development of a New Historical Field” (1985); “Environmental History, Ecology, and Meaning” (1990); The Middle Ground: Indians, Empires, and Republics in the Great Lakes Region, 1650–1815 (1991); The Organic Machine: The Remaking of the Columbia River (1995); “‘Are You an Environmentalist or Do You Work for a Living?’” (1995). Readings: Savard (1992), Edmunds (1993) and D. R. Miller (1994) on The Middle Ground; Cronon's foreword (1992) to Land Use. Later and additional selected works: “It’s Your Misfortune and None of My Own”: A New History of the American West (1991); Remembering Ahanagran: Storytelling in a Family’s Past (1998; Washington paperback as A History of Stories, 2003, foreword by William Cronon); “The Nationalization of Nature” (1999); “What is Spatial History?” (2010 working paper); Railroaded: The Transcontinentals and the Making of Modern America (2011); The Republic for Which It Stands (2017); California Exposures: Envisioning Myth and History (documented in 2020, photographs by Jesse Amble White); Who Killed Jane Stanford? (2022).
node.scope_note: Not Hayden White (node white). Witnesses for The Middle Ground: Cambridge Core first-page excerpts (full pages, folios observed) of the introduction (1991 p. ix) and of the chapters opening at pp. 50, 94 and 518; the next page of the introduction (1991 p. x = 2011 p. xxvi) and pp. 52–53 and 93 only in Google Books search-within snippets of the 2011 twentieth-anniversary edition, whose body pagination matches 1991 at the pages checked (the equation 1991 p. x = 2011 p. xxvi is inferred from the introduction's opening at 1991 p. ix and 2011 p. xxv). The rest of the book is unread, and wording witnessed only by snippets is paraphrased in node text. Land Use (1980; 1992 paperback) and The Organic Machine (1995) are known from Google Books search-within snippets of their framing pages, not from page images; The Organic Machine's preface folios were not visible, so its framing is paraphrased. The Roots of Dependency (1983), the 1985 survey, the 1990 round-table response and the 1995 Uncommon Ground essay are unread (paywalled or not previewed) and are known through Cronon (1993, 1994), Worster (1990, Portuguese translation), Cook (1990), Isenberg (2013) and the publisher's records. He is not presented as a founder of environmental history: Land Use credits James Malin's neglected Great Plains studies as a trail to follow (snippet, p. 7), and Isenberg (2013) names him in a group of synthesisers. The middle ground was contested in period: Savard (1992) doubts its premise of Iroquois devastation, Edmunds (1993) finds the post-1770 chapters 'less convincing', and D. R. Miller (1994) notes the neglect of peoples neither Iroquoian nor Algonquian; Merrell's in-period critique (Into the American Woods, 1999) is known here only through White's later 2011 response. Havard (2003) and Deloria (2006) are later critiques, also known here only through that 2011 preface, a later reading. Canadian environmental historians cite him chiefly for the 1985 survey; Canadian use of The Middle Ground before 2000 is checked only in reviews and one legal article. incident_edges.relationship: The middle ground: accommodation through mutual invention and creative misunderstanding between Algonquian villages and empires in the Great Lakes region, 1650–1815 (1991)
incident_edges.evidence_note: White's own statement, The Middle Ground (1991). Introduction, p. ix (Cambridge Core first-page excerpt: the full page, folio observed): histories of Indian–white relations have had 'but two outcomes', stories 'of conquest and assimilation' or 'of cultural persistence'; their tellers 'miss a larger process and a larger truth. The meeting of sea and continent, like the meeting of whites and Indians, creates as well as destroys.' The next page (1991 p. x = 2011 p. xxvi; witnessed only by Google Books search-within snippets of the 2011 edition, page images not seen, the 1991 page inferred) defines the middle ground, in paraphrase, as the space between cultures, between peoples, and between empires and the stateless world of villages, where differences were accommodated through creative and often expedient misunderstanding, and explains it by the long periods in which whites could neither command Indians nor ignore them. Chapter 2 opening (p. 50, Cambridge Core first-page excerpt, folio observed): French and Algonquians 'had to arrive at some common conception of suitable ways of acting; they had to create what I have already referred to as a middle ground. The creation of the middle ground involved a process of mutual invention by both the French and the Algonquians.' It rested on 'the need of people to find a means, other than force, to gain the cooperation or consent of foreigners' (p. 52), and was, in paraphrase, a product both of everyday life and of formal diplomacy between distinct peoples (p. 53) (both Google Books search-within snippets of the 2011 edition; page numbers as the snippet results give them, taken to match 1991). Chapter 3 opening (p. 94, Cambridge Core first-page excerpt): the fur trade was 'a constantly changing compromise, a conduit, between two local models of the exchange'. Epilogue (p. 518, Cambridge Core first-page excerpt): 'The compromises intrinsic in the middle ground yielded to stark choices between assimilation and otherness.' In-period reception, each read in full. Savard (1992; Université de Montréal anthropologist) judges the book's circularity 'inattaquable' and suited to 'bien d'autres époques et régions de l'Amérique du Nord', but asks whether the Algonquians' shattered prior state and Iroquois military supremacy, 'cet autre mythe fondateur de la république américaine', were needed to explain it (p. 120). Edmunds (1993) calls the thesis 'a valuable model for the exploration of the Indian-French relationship' (p. 148) and the book possibly 'a landmark volume in the ethnohistory of the Great Lakes tribes', but finds 'his arguments for the period after 1770 are less convincing' (p. 149). D. R. Miller (1994, Canadian Journal of Native Studies, from the Saskatchewan Indian Federated College) calls it 'an extraordinary benchmark in the scholarship of European and Aboriginal relations' (p. 157), notes that White 'deemphasizes the specificity of a small number of groups in the larger Great Lakes region that are neither Iroquoian or Algonquian' (p. 158), and writes that 'The challenge for a similar study with emphasis upon the north side of the Great Lakes is obvious' (p. 170). The edge records a scholar's interpretation of Indigenous–imperial relations, which the Indigenous history entry lists as related scholarship; it does not make the work an Indigenous historical practice or a source of Indigenous authority. Later readings, not evidence for this edge: White's 2011 preface (Google Books search-within snippets only) answers Merrell's in-period critique (Into the American Woods, 1999; cited pp. xx–xxi) and the later critiques of Havard (Empire et métissages, 2003; p. xvi) and Deloria ('What Is the Middle Ground, Anyway?', 2006; cited p. xii; both unread here): the middle ground 'did not involve the achievement of a widespread mutual understanding and appreciation between Europeans and Indian peoples. People did not come together to love one another' (p. xxi), and he did not think that 'every time you find this process at work you would find the construction of a coherent space that is the equivalent of pays d'en haut' (p. xiii). McNeill (2003; text-layer PDF) reports that the concept 'struck historians of Japan and medieval Austria as useful for their own studies' (p. 37).

incident_edges.relationship: Environmental change through land use, subsistence and labour: Island County (1980), the roots of Native dependency (1983) and the Columbia as an organic machine (1995), with an early survey of the field (1985)
incident_edges.evidence_note: White's own statements, known for his books only through Google Books search-within snippets (page images not seen) and therefore paraphrased where the wording carries the claim. Land Use, Environment, and Social Change (1980; snippets of the 1992 paperback, whose body text is the 1980 text; p. 7 as given in the snippet results): White presents the book as departing somewhat from recent environmental history, which he describes as mostly a variant of intellectual and political history, by tracing the environmental impact of Indian and later intruding peoples and its consequences for their societies; on the same page he credits James Malin's Great Plains studies, ignored by most historians, as a trail to follow. In the preface to the 1992 edition (November 1991; snippet, folio xviii inferred from Google Books page ids that carry the printed folios xi, xvi and xvii) he judges his own use of ecology: 'I used ecological concepts like community, succession, climax, and ecosystem unproblematically even though within the discipline of ecology those ideas had already come under attack'. Cronon's foreword (October 1991; snippets, folio xi observed) places the book among White's contributions 'to environmental history, to the history of the American West, to Indian history, and to American history generally' and calls it 'a textbook case of an underappreciated classic' (p. xi). The Organic Machine (1995; snippets of the preface, whose printed folios were not visible, and of the conclusion, p. 112 taken from the Google Books page id, not seen as a printed folio), in paraphrase: White examines the Columbia as an organic machine, an energy system modified by human intervention that keeps natural, unmade qualities; human labour is energy as much as the river's flow or the calories salmon store for their journey; environmentalists, he argues, distance humans from nature by favouring the eye over the hand and contemplation over work; and the conclusion finds the nature in us in our labour and energy (p. 112). In-period third-party readings: Cronon (1993; OCR of the author-hosted page scan) footnotes Land Use and The Roots of Dependency (nn. 15, 23) for the lesson that 'the horse was not simply a European invader, but a complex cultural entity' (p. 9); D. R. Miller (1994; PDF read in full) calls him 'The social and environmental historian Richard White' (p. 157) and quotes The Middle Ground that dependency 'is an economic, political, and social relationship, but can also be an environmental relationship' (p. 169). On the 1985 survey (unread; paywalled): Worster (1990, read in the 2002–03 Portuguese translation, n. 5, p. 42) calls it the best effort to trace the field's emergence, 'pelo menos em uma parte influente do mundo', reporting White's view that frontier and western history was the formative influence; Cronon's 1994 graduate syllabus assigns it 'read for main themes' (p. 4); in Canada, Cook (1990) cites it (n. 4) for Turner and Webb as 'important, if declining, influences into the 1950s' (p. 6). A contribution, not a founding. Later readings, not evidence for this edge: Isenberg (2013) names White among historians who 'synthesized the material and cultural approaches to the environment' (p. 87) and quotes his 1990 round-table objection that Worster's scheme reduced culture to 'superstructure in the old vulgar Marxist sense' (pp. 88–89, citing JAH 76, pp. 1112–1113; the JAH text is unread).

incident_edges.relationship: DuVal: in the Arkansas Valley Native peoples dominated and incorporated colonists; 'only relatively weak people desired the kind of compromises inherent in a middle ground' (2006)
incident_edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents Kathleen DuVal's argument (The Native Ground, 2006), not a verdict of the field. Introduction unread; the central sentence, p. 5, is witnessed identically by two readers read here: Piker (AHR 112:3, 2007, extract read) and Isaac (ActiveHistory, 2021, read in full). Piker also quotes p. 5: colonialism 'met neither accommodation nor resistance but incorporation'. Hatfield (Common-Place 7:2, 2007, read in full): DuVal 'argues that unlike the peoples of the Great Lakes region Richard White studies … Arkansas Indians dominated their region well into the nineteenth century … because they were not a population of refugees as were the Indians in the Great Lakes'. White's side, in his own words: a middle ground needs 'a rough balance of power, mutual need … and an inability by either side to commandeer enough force to compel the other to change' (2006, p. 10, as quoted in English by Avila 2011, p. 272). (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-older-scholarship.md §1.4)

incident_edges.relationship: Witgen: in a Native New World the French moved, as Reda puts it, from misunderstanding to being 'essentially delusional' about their relations; European possession of the interior 'never occurred' (2012)
incident_edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents Michael Witgen's book as read by John Reda (H-AmIndian, July 2014, read in full), p. 2: 'Up to this point, Witgen's explanation seems little different from Richard White's middle ground, where cultural misinterpretations often led to workable understandings between Europeans and Native Americans. Witgen, however, pushes further to demonstrate that the French passed quickly from misunderstanding Native Americans to becoming essentially delusional about the nature of their relationships with them.' Witgen as quoted by Reda: 'the possession of large portions of Native North America by the empires of Europe never occurred' (p. 28); the British 'simply inherited the illusion of empire' (p. 217). 'Delusional' is Reda's word, not Witgen's. The book is unread. White's side, in his own words: a middle ground needs 'a rough balance of power, mutual need … and an inability by either side to commandeer enough force to compel the other to change' (2006, p. 10, as quoted in English by Avila 2011, p. 272). (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-older-scholarship.md §1.6)

incident_edges.relationship: White in 2021 (interview published in Portuguese translation): the more anthropology he read, the more critical he became of ethnohistory as a hybrid, and he is increasingly wary of upstreaming; the New Indian History now looks primitive, and its agency argument could go too far
incident_edges.evidence_note: Paraphrase only. Fontella, História (São Paulo) 41 (2022), e2022054 (read in full): White's English answers, received 30 April 2021, are published only in Fontella's Portuguese translation, so no English words are attributed to him. p. 10: 'quanto mais Antropologia eu lia, mais crítico eu me tornava do híbrido: Etnohistória'; 'A New Indian History parece bastante primitiva agora … a tendência poderia ir longe demais, disfarçando as enormes forças que muitas vezes matavam muitos deles e destruíam suas sociedades'; p. 15: 'estou cada vez mais desconfiado do upstreaming'; p. 16: upstreaming assumes that a belief, ritual or practice 'contém um significado inato que não muda significativamente à medida que viaja no tempo'. The later worry about agency is his own; it is not evidence about Brownlie and Kelm's 1994 essay. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-older-scholarship.md §1.1)

named_group_routes.relationship: Prakash defends deconstruction for postcolonial historical writing against O'Hanlon and Washbrook's charge of a 'residual positivism' (1992)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Gyan Prakash, 'Can the “Subaltern” Ride?' (CSSH 1992; Verso reprint, pp. 224–227, read), defends deconstruction for historical writing under the heading 'Deconstructive Criticism and Historical Writing', reading Derrida's Of Grammatology and 'White Mythology' and answering O'Hanlon and Washbrook, who, as he quotes them, charge it with a 'residual positivism' and, in his paraphrase, with treating the historian's intervention in the past as illegitimate (p. 225, citing their p. 198, 2000 reprint pagination). O'Hanlon and Washbrook's own text is known here only through its first page and notes (pe132_ohanlon_washbrook_1992) and through Prakash's quotations. Rosalind O'Hanlon (1988; reprint p. 80, read) reads the Subaltern series' recovery of the subject as a 'strategy' whose 'limitations have yet to receive any proper public discussion'. Spivak's own use is the separate derrida → Spivak edge.

named_group_routes.relationship: Annales geography and multiple time scales as a source of ideas and a temporal affinity for environmental history, acknowledged by Worster (1990) and Cronon (1993); McNeill (2003) later reassessed the Annales treatment of environmental change while crediting their general approach as inspirational
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period acknowledgements first. Donald Worster, 'Transformations of the Earth' (JAH 1990), note 5. Witnesses: the Portuguese translation (Ambiente & Sociedade 5:2/6:1, 2002–03, p. 42, n. 5; PDF read in full) and Internet Archive full-text-search snippets of Worster's 1993 reprint in The Wealth of Nature (ch. 4, n. 5; p. 226 inferred from the running heads on either side; page images not seen; whether the reprint revised the note was not checked). The English JAH page was not reached. Because the English wording is known only from joined search snippets, it is given here as paraphrase: after reporting White's view that frontier and western history had been the formative influence on the field, Worster names French historians and geographers associated with Annales, particularly Braudel, Febvre and Le Roy Ladurie, as a further important source of ideas, distinct from the Turnerian tradition. The translation reads: 'Uma outra fonte de idéias importante, realmente retirada da influência de Frederick Jackson Turner, tem sido a dos historiadores e geógrafos franceses, particularmente Fernand Braudel, Lucien Febvre e Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie, todos associados à revista dos Annales' (p. 42, n. 5). William Cronon, 'The Uses of Environmental History' (1993; OCR of the author-hosted page scan, journal pagination), p. 14: 'Perhaps this is why we feel some kinship with a Braudelian vision of history in which the different time scales of la longue durée, la vie matérielle, and l'histoire événementielle weave together to form the tapestry of the past. Although our general bias is often toward the longue durée, we understand that the interactions of environment, economy, political institutions, social norms, cultural values, and natural processes are endlessly complex' (n. 29 cites The Mediterranean). Both acknowledge a source of ideas and a kinship, not a lineage, and neither disputes it. Later reading, not evidence for the 1990–93 claim: J. R. McNeill (2003; text-layer PDF, p. 14 re-read) reassesses the Annales treatment of environmental change, writing that 'the Annales historians were, many of them, strangely blind to evolving environments'; Braudel 'normally imagined it as an unchanging force', while Le Roy Ladurie 'embraced environmental change'; 'To a very limited extent, then, Annales historians were engaged in environmental history avant la lettre'; yet 'Their general approach however proved inspirational for many who would become environmental historians'. Gurevich's chapter (publisher abstract only) supports the Annales side: geography among the school's concerns; it says nothing about environmental history. Earlier wording (an undirected comparison of affinities) is replaced because Worster and Cronon describe influence running from the Annales to the field, not a comparison between equals.
