named_group_routes.relationship: Narrative bounded by evidence, ecology and the community of scholars: an environmental historian’s answer to postmodern critiques of narrative (1992); twenty years on, 'Storytelling' (2013) restated the case: 'How do we make the past come alive? By telling stories about it', referring readers to the 1992 essay for 'this theoretical background'
named_group_routes.evidence_note: 'A Place for Stories: Nature, History, and Narrative', JAH 78:4 (March 1992), author-hosted copy in journal pagination (pp. 1347–1351 and 1369–1376 read). Writing about narrative, 'we cannot avoid encountering the postmodernist assault on narrative, which calls into question not just the stories we tell but the deeper purpose that motivated us in the first place' (p. 1349). The argument is meant for all historians: 'I am urging historians to acknowledge storytelling as the necessary core even of longue durée histories … Environmental history is but one example of these, and most of my arguments apply just as readily to the others' (p. 1349, n. 5). 'I, like most practicing historians, am only willing to follow the postmodernists so far'; 'My goal throughout has been to acknowledge the immense power of narrative while still defending the past (and nature) as real things to which our storytelling must somehow conform lest it cease being history altogether' (p. 1372). Three bounds: 'our stories cannot contravene known facts about the past' and 'our stories must make ecological sense' (p. 1372); 'We write as members of communities' (p. 1373). 'To just that extent, nature coauthors our stories' (p. 1373). Against 'an endless postmodernist deconstruction of texts that fails to ground itself in history, in community, in politics, and finally in the moral problem of living on earth' he asserts 'the virtues of narrative' (p. 1374), and he asks environmental historians for 'not just stories about nature, but stories about stories about nature' (p. 1375). He reads with Hayden White’s Metahistory, Tropics of Discourse and The Content of the Form and with Novick (nn. 6, 7, 43), and credits Richard White with the argument about criticism (n. 46). The 1993 address restates it: historical wisdom 'usually comes in the form of parables, not policy recommendations or certainties' (p. 16). This is his own text; no in-period reading that places the essay in the postmodernism debate was read. Period-4 wave 1 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md) (edge_903 revision): the 2013 address read in passages (AHA open text; n. 14 refers to 'A Place for Stories').

named_group_routes.relationship: Three levels of environmental history (nature, modes of production, ideas), with the capitalist transformation of agriculture as the middle level (1979–1990); and, at the end, the 'Second Earth' of 1500 whose abundance gave 'the false impression that there was no limit' (Shrinking the Earth, 2016, as read by Collomb)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Worster's own statements, in-period first. 'Appendix: Doing Environmental History', The Ends of the Earth (1988), read in an abridged reprint and checked by full-text search of the 1988 edition, whose running heads place the passage between pp. 292 and 294 (Isenberg 2013 cites p. 293): 'There are three levels on which the new history proceeds, three clusters of issues it addresses'; 'The first deals with understanding nature itself, as organized and functioning in past times'; 'The second level in this history brings in the socioeconomic realm as it interacts with the environment. Here we are concerned with tools and work, with the social relations that grow out of that work, with the various modes people have devised of producing goods from natural resources'; the third is 'the purely mental or intellectual, in which perceptions, ethics, laws, myths, and other structures of meaning become part of an individual's or group's dialogue with nature'; together they 'constitute a single dynamic inquiry'. 'Transformations of the Earth' (JAH 1990; English text checked in Worster's 1993 reprint in The Wealth of Nature, ch. 4; JAH page as cited by Isenberg): 'most environmental historians seem to have settled philosophically on a position that is at once materialist and idealist', yet the essay turns to 'that middle level, the analysis of modes of production as ecological phenomena' (p. 1091), and proposes that 'the single most important task for scholars in the history of modern agroecology is to trace what Karl Polanyi has called “the great transformation”'. Dust Bowl (1979) had argued: 'Capitalism, it is my contention, has been the decisive factor in this nation's use of nature' (p. 5, as quoted by Cronon 1992, p. 1363; wording confirmed in the 1979 edition). In-period readings: Merchant's 1990 response (read) calls his 'conceptual levels of ecology (natural history), production (technology and its socioeconomic relations), and cognition' 'a significant framework for research and writing in this emerging field', while the essay 'lacks a gender analysis' and environmental history 'needs a fourth analytical level, that of reproduction' (p. 1117). Cronon (1992, read) finds that in Dust Bowl 'the chief agent of the story is not “the pioneers” or “civilization” or “man”; it is capitalism', a plot that 'proclaims an apocalyptic prophecy' (p. 1363). McDean (1986) criticises the generalisation across the Plains (existing source, not re-read). A contribution, not a founding: Worster takes the idea from Aldo Leopold, who 'spoke of “an ecological interpretation of history”' (1988), and McEvoy's ecology, production and cognition triad appeared in the same 1988 volume. Later readings, not evidence for this edge: Isenberg (2013, pp. 88–89) reports White's and Cronon's 1990 objections ('superstructure in the old vulgar Marxist sense'; 'potentially excessive materialism'), whose texts are unread here; McNeill (2003, p. 37) writes of environmental historians' theories that 'The most cogent was probably the one elaborated in slightly different versions by both Donald Worster and Arthur McEvoy', but that such theories 'have sparked no groundswells of enthusiasm'. Period-4 wave 1 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md) (edge_904 revision): Collomb 2017 para. 2 read in full; Shrinking the Earth itself unread; the Origins page (Hall chair from 1989 until retirement) and the AHA award list (2012) read.

named_group_routes.relationship: Silent Spring as a catalyst for environmental concern, read by US environmental historians as a starting point and a shared text (1962; readings 1971–1994)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Witnesses. Opie (1971), Worster (1977), Dunlap (1981), Hays (1987) and Nash (1989) were read only through the Internet Archive's full-text search of borrow-only scans: passages were rebuilt from overlapping search snippets and the page images were not seen, so their wording is given here as attributed paraphrase. Pages marked 'running head' were observed in the snippets; pages marked 'by the index' are inferred. In-period readings first. (1) John Opie, ed., Americans and Environment: The Controversy over Ecology (D. C. Heath, Problems in American Civilization, 1971). Opie taught at Duquesne and founded ASEH in 1977 (ASEH history page). His introduction (p. x, between running heads) dates the modern controversy over human use of the earth to the publication of Silent Spring, which he misdates to 1960, and describes it as an essay on the irreversible damage pesticides had done to the balance of nature. Part II, 'The Contemporary Controversy Begins', opens with Carson, 'Biology or Oblivion?' (from p. 67), followed by Frank Graham Jr., 'The Resulting Outcry' (from p. 91) (contents). (2) Donald Worster, Nature's Economy (1977), credits her as the nature writer who did more than anyone to launch the recent ecology movement, and says that with Silent Spring she began a literature of ecological apocalypse (pp. 23–24, by the index); the chapter 'The Age of Ecology' (from p. 339) presents Silent Spring as showing that persistent pesticides threatened life less obviously than, and perhaps as gravely as, the atomic bomb (p. 340, between running heads 339 and 341). (3) Thomas R. Dunlap, DDT: Scientists, Citizens, and Public Policy (1981), introduction: DDT stayed a quiet issue until Silent Spring touched off a heated debate in 1962 by attacking both the chemicals and the experts who recommended them (pp. 3–4, running head), turning a quiet scientific discussion into a noisy public one (p. 7, running head); chapter 5 is 'Storm over Silent Spring'. (4) ASEH history page (an undated later account of a 1980 event; web text read): at the April 1980 Denver conference, Opie asked participants for lists of influential titles but told them 'to omit Lynn White, Jr., Roderick Nash, Clarence Glacken, Aldo Leopold, Rachel Carson, … authors whose works Opie assumed his interlocutors had all already read'. (5) Samuel P. Hays, in collaboration with Barbara D. Hays, Beauty, Health, and Permanence (1987), chapter 'The Toxic Environment': the pesticide problem gained wide public attention when Carson published Silent Spring on the dangers of pesticides to wildlife (pp. 174–75, running head). (6) Roderick Nash, The Rights of Nature (1989), sets Silent Spring beside Uncle Tom's Cabin as a book that exploded against traditional American assumptions and calls it a landmark of an ecological perspective (p. 78, by the index). (7) William Cronon, History 901 syllabus (Fall 1994; archived PDF read): Silent Spring is on the bookstore list of 'central texts' (p. 2) and is assigned, pp. 1–37, 103–27 and 187–98, for the 30 November session 'Toxic Politics' (p. 6). These readings show Silent Spring as a catalyst for environmental concern and a text US environmental historians shared; none of them says that it founded or catalysed environmental history as a discipline. Her framework, from Silent Spring (2002 Mariner edition, OCR text of a partial page scan with running heads; Worster's notes cite the same sentences at pp. 8 and 297, so the pagination matches 1962 at those points): 'The most alarming of all man’s assaults upon the environment is the contamination of air, earth, rivers, and sea with dangerous and even lethal materials' (p. 6); 'They should not be called “insecticides,” but “biocides”' (p. 8); 'They reflect the web of life — or death — that scientists know as ecology' (p. 189); 'The “control of nature” is a phrase conceived in arrogance, born of the Neanderthal age of biology and philosophy, when it was supposed that nature exists for the convenience of man' (p. 297). Later readings, labelled: the claim that Silent Spring advanced the discipline itself is Jane Carruthers's (2004, open PDF), a later and geographically qualified reading. She lists it among the stimuli to which 'the social sciences responded enthusiastically, history among them' (p. 380), and reports that Grove 'conceded that Carson’s Silent Spring had been critical to advancing the discipline' in the United States only (p. 383). Cronon's c. 2004–05 reading list puts it first under 'Classics and Precursors' (p. 1). An influence, not a founding. Criticism is recorded in the scope note: industry attacks in 1962, Dunlap's judgement that she had done no original research (p. 7), and Nash on her anthropocentrism (p. 80).
named_group_routes.map_label: Shared reading in US environmental history, 1971–94

named_group_routes.relationship: ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’: the two senses of representation, the epistemic violence of colonial law and knowledge, and the subaltern woman silenced between colonial and indigenous patriarchal discourse on sati (1985–99)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements. ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988), read in the Williams and Chrisman reprint (pages of that reprint; its opening is abridged): ‘Some of the most radical criticism coming out of the West today is the result of an interested desire to conserve the subject of the West, or the West as Subject’ (p. 66). ‘Two senses of representation are being run together: representation as “speaking for”, as in politics, and representation as “re-presentation”, as in art or philosophy’; ‘representing them, the intellectuals represent themselves as transparent’ (p. 70); running vertreten and darstellen together ‘leads to an essentialist, utopian politics’ (p. 71). The codification of Hindu law is her ‘example of epistemic violence’ (pp. 76–77), and she asks whether, ‘inside and outside the circuit of the epistemic violence of imperialist law and education’, ‘can the subaltern speak?’ (p. 78). On sati she sets the sentence ‘White men are saving brown women from brown men’, which she says she ‘put together’ (p. 92), against ‘the Indian nativist argument’, ‘“The women actually wanted to die”’: ‘The two sentences go a long way to legitimize each other. One never encounters the testimony of the women’s voice-consciousness’ (p. 93). She qualifies: ‘Given that the abolition of sati was in itself admirable’ (p. 94); ‘Obviously I am not advocating the killing of widows’ (p. 97). ‘Between patriarchy and imperialism, subject-constitution and object-formation, the figure of the woman disappears ... into a violent shuttling’ (p. 102). She welcomes ‘all the information retrieval in these silenced areas’ in history and other disciplines, while warning that the assumed ‘consciousness or subject’ will ‘cohere with the work of imperialist subject-constitution’ (p. 90). The close: ‘The subaltern cannot speak. There is no virtue in global laundry lists with “woman” as a pious item. Representation has not withered away’ (reprint p. 104, wording restored from the unpaginated 1988 text in Morris, 2010; 1988 p. 308 per Sunder Rajan in the same volume). She credits Lata Mani’s 1983 thesis on sati as ‘a brilliant account’ and ‘profited from discussion with Ms Mani’ (n. 65, p. 109). The 1999 revision (A Critique of Postcolonial Reason, ch. 3; read in Morris’s unpaginated reprint; CPR p. 308 per Sunder Rajan) says: ‘in the first version of this text, I wrote, in the accents of passionate lament: the subaltern cannot speak! It was an inadvisable remark’, and that Bhubaneswari Bhaduri ‘was not a “true” subaltern’. ‘Three Women’s Texts’ (Critical Inquiry, 1985, read pp. 243–245) opens: ‘It should not be possible to read nineteenth-century British literature without remembering that imperialism, understood as England’s social mission, was a crucial part of the cultural representation of England to the English’, and finds it ‘particularly unfortunate when the emergent perspective of feminist criticism reproduces the axioms of imperialism’ (p. 243). In-period readings by historians: Gyan Prakash, ‘Can the “Subaltern” Ride?’ (CSSH 1992; Verso reprint 2000, pp. 226–227, read): ‘as Spivak states starkly, the debate left no room for the woman’s enunciatory position’; ‘Spivak very correctly marks the silencing of the subaltern woman as the point at which the interpreter must acknowledge the limits of historical understanding’. Sumit Sarkar, ‘Orientalism Revisited’ (Oxford Literary Review, 1994; reprint p. 254, n. 14, read), criticising Mani’s Saidian assumptions, contrasts ‘the much more substantive discussion of pre-colonial and colonial discourses on sati in Spivak’. Contested in period: Terry Eagleton (LRB, 13 May 1999; web text, no page numbers, read) on A Critique of Postcolonial Reason: ‘too well-mannered, as well as too episodic’ to be the critique its title promises, ‘too deeply invested in feminism and post-colonialism to launch a full-scale socialist critique of these currents’, yet ‘this study boldly addresses the economic realities which too many post-colonial critics culturalise away’; he reports that she contrasts her own critique with Aijaz Ahmad’s ‘scorching assault’ in In Theory (1992; unread here). Benita Parry, ‘Problems in Current Theories of Colonial Discourse’, Oxford Literary Review 9 (1987), pp. 27–58, is the best-known in-period critique; it is closed access and unread, and no claim is made about its argument. A contribution, not a founding: the post entry already lists Said (1978) before her, and edge_107 (language → post) and edge_115 (subaltern → post) stay. Later reception, added in revision 1.151: Interventions 4:2 (2002) devoted a special issue to A Critique of Postcolonial Reason, from a panel at the IAPL conference in 2000, with her response (metadata and abstracts only); Mark Sanders's abstract holds that placing "Can the subaltern speak?" in the book's "History" chapter "emphasizes its deconstruction of Marxist politics". Ritu Birla's abstract (the essay is unread) explores "the challenges of radical history writing" through the book's chapter on history, under the themes of "limits, the open secret, and value/transvaluation"; it sets Spivak beside Joan Scott's critique of "experience", opening "a discussion of the supplementary relationship of literature and history", and connects the limit of history to "the selective production of the archive".

named_group_routes.relationship: Women and marriage à la façon du pays at the centre of fur-trade society, and missionary racism against Native wives in Red River (1980–86)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period. 'Many Tender Ties' (1980) is unread here and is quoted only as Bowsfield quotes it (Archivaria 12, 1981, review article, read in full; he gives no page references to the book). He reports her purpose as showing that the fur trade 'constituted a social and cultural complex as well as an economic activity'. He quotes her claims that 'If a man formed a liaison with a woman she was considered to be his wife, entitled to the recognition and support that a marital relationship implied' and that Indian women's work 'constituted an important contribution to the functioning of the trade'. He paraphrases her account of a marriage rite à la façon du pays and of the later turn from Indian to mixed-descent and then white wives, as younger officers became 'imbued with the Victorian middle-class desire for respectability and success' (p. 124). Gagan and Turner (Archivaria 14, 1982, read in full) summarise her argument that these marriages, 'generations of scandalized references notwithstanding, were crucial to the establishment of early western society' (p. 43). Her own words, 1986 (Manitoba History 11, web edition, read in full; no page numbers): 'Fur trade society in Rupert's Land had resulted from decades of inter-marriage among incoming white fur traders with Indian and later mixed-blood women'; 'Racist attitudes, particularly with regard to women, can be seen in the attempts of the missionaries to enforce their concepts of morality upon a society that had developed its own indigenous customs.' Brown (Canadian Journal of Native Studies 3:1, 1983, read in full) takes 'the work of Sylvia Van Kirk (1980) on the socioeconomic role of women in the fur trade' as one starting point for Métis history (p. 40). Criticism: Bowsfield notes her view that such unions were not 'casual' or 'promiscuous' and comments, 'This may be too complimentary a picture of both native women and European men' (p. 124). LaRocque's criticism (1999) is recorded on pe139_vankirk_rel_04, and edge_868 carries the Indigenous critiques at entry level. Not a founding: Bowsfield reviews the book within a fur-trade literature already recast by Ray, Trigger and others (pp. 121–24). Later reading, labelled: Perry (Left History 13:2, 2008, read in full) writes that 'In the early 1990s Van Kirk's work particularly garnered some sharp post-colonial, anti-racist, and post-structuralist critiques, ones that made clear how wedded "Many Tender Ties" was to a Eurocentric, celebratory sort of liberal feminism', and then that Van Kirk's and Brown's 'symbiotic arguments about the centrality of women and family to the Canadian fur-trade' have 'never been cast into serious doubt' (p. 163). The critiques she cites (n. 7: Pierson 1992; Emberley 1990–91) are unread here.

named_group_routes.relationship: Indigenous and mixed-descent women written into Canadian women's history, with race as a division among women (1980–98)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period. As Bowsfield quotes the book (Archivaria 12, 1981, p. 124; no page given), Van Kirk claimed that it 'supports the claims of theorists in women's history that sex roles should constitute a category of historical investigation', and she admitted the limits of relying on male sources. He finds 'a feminist note to some of Van Kirk's statements but it must be admitted that it is not a strident one'. Gagan and Turner's survey of Canadian social history (Archivaria 14, 1982, p. 29 and n. 7) puts 'Many Tender Ties' and Strangers in Blood under women's work: 'two noteworthy recent studies attempt to recreate the whole way of life of a particular group of "working" women, those who participated in the Canadian fur trade', in which 'the whole woman-wife, mother, labourer, diplomat, chattel, entrepreneur-is revealed'. Her own words, 1986 (Manitoba History 11, read in full): 'Other important themes for women's history also emerge'; 'The reasons for such "unsisterly" action should be confronted squarely by feminist historians'; 'The rivalry among women in nineteenth century Red River, however, was compounded by the issue of race'; and 'The racism evinced by white women in Red River, while as inexcusable as that of their male counterparts, was aggravated by what, in their view, was a concrete threat to their own welfare in the competition for eligible husbands.' 1997–98 (BC Studies 115/116, pp. 149–51 read): 'Little attention has been paid to the fact that this process of acculturation was gendered'; 'a complex interaction of gender and class dynamics, coupled with the particular demographics of early Victoria, enabled the girls to transcend the racist climate of the colony more successfully than the boys' (p. 150). Reception in a Canadian women's studies journal, 2000 (Atlantis 25:1, both read in full): McPherson calls the book a 'now-classic work' and writes that 'Van Kirk's research and the critical debates it has aroused have played a crucial role in writing Native women into western Canadian history and in bringing cultural difference and conflict into Canadian women's history' (p. 82). Fiske writes that understanding the discursive formation of Aboriginal women's sexuality 'requires us to build on the early work of Sylvia Van Kirk (1980) and Jennifer Brown (1980) by placing Aboriginal women in the context of the expectations held of settler women' (p. 12); this extends the work rather than rejecting it. Pierson's 'Colonization and Canadian Women's History' (1992) cites the book (OpenAlex reference list only; text unread). Criticism is recorded on rel_01 (Bowsfield) and rel_04 (LaRocque). edge_872 compares the two field entries at title level; this edge adds her own words and the field's reading of her.

named_group_routes.relationship: Company families compared, and women and descent in Métis emergence: Hudson's Bay and North West Company fathers, mothers and children (1980–85)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period. Strangers in Blood (1980) is unread here. Gresko (Canadian Woman Studies 3:2, 1981, read in full) quotes the book's double sense of its title: the British legal term for 'any relationship, even familial that the law refused to admit as legitimate', and 'one way of characterizing the meetings of Whites and Indians ... in the fur trade of North America'. She reports that before 1821 the two companies, despite 'their common British (and heavily Scottish) facade', built different social organisations in Indian country. She quotes Brown that later social distinctions were 'strongly related to changing economic pressures' and that old Nor'Westers tended 'not to assume an active paternal role' (pp. 112–13). Bowsfield (Archivaria 12, 1981) singles out the 'comparison between Hudson's Bay Company and North West Company men as husbands and fathers', which Brown relates partly to 'the relationship of hinterland to metropolis' (p. 124). Her own words come from a paper to the Métis symposium held in Winnipeg in November 1982 (Canadian Journal of Native Studies 3:1, 1983, read in full). 'Biologically, métissage in North America can be described in a unitary way, as the meeting and mingling of Indian and white racial groups. Socially and culturally, it has had a complex history over many generations' (p. 40). Among Nor'Westers who had children baptized in Montreal, 1796–1821, sons were favoured 'by a margin of about two to one', so daughters 'were more likely by a two-to-one margin to remain in the Indian country, marrying there and contributing to the very rapid growth of biracial population' (p. 41). Coltman, Pambrun and McGillivray in 1818 'were all in accord in calling attention to the maternal element as formative in metis emergence' (p. 44). 'It is all too easy to learn more about the men than the women' (p. 45). The essay cites The New Peoples, then forthcoming from the 1981 Newberry Library Conference on the Metis; the 1985 collection itself is title-level here. Criticism. Gresko finds the book 'still too much in the form of the academic thesis' and 'complicated by seemingly insignificant bits of anthropological theory', and notes that it does not mention Jamieson's Indian Women and the Law in Canada (1978) (p. 113). LaRocque (1999, PDF p. 249) names Brown in the 'neo cross-cultural approach' that she criticises (see pe139_vankirk_rel_04 and edge_868). Not a founding: in 1983 she places her questions beside Jacqueline Peterson's (1981, 1982) and Van Kirk's (1980) (p. 40). Later readings, labelled. Gaudry (aboriginal policy studies 2:2, 2013, read in full) uses Peterson and Brown (1985) for the distinction between 'small-m métis', 'mixed Indigenous and European from a diversity of backgrounds', and 'big-M Métis', 'descended from the Red River Métis people, the New Nation'. With Andersen (2011, as Gaudry quotes him; unread), he rejects reducing 'the astonishing complexity of Red River Métis to their ostensible mixedness' (p. 78). He does not attribute that reduction to Peterson and Brown. In the 2017 reprint of her 1985 essay, Brown drops 'Presbyterian Métis' from the title. 'The term "Métis," as used in Rupert's Land in the 1800s, referred particularly to Roman Catholics of French Canadian paternal origin', and the children 'cannot be subsumed under any one label' (pp. 145–46).

named_group_routes.relationship: Anthropological models brought to fur-trade, court and mission records for Métis, Cree and Ojibwe history (1983–96)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period, her own words. The 1983 essay (Canadian Journal of Native Studies 3:1, read in full) reads fur-trade sources through anthropological models. Bishop and Krech's argument for early subarctic 'matriorganization' leads her to ask 'whether native women in emergent metis groups looked for and found ways to maintain this organizational bias in their own families and social lives' (p. 40). She tests Asch's 'unilocality' among the Slavey against fur-trade families (p. 42), using the HBC district report on Île-à-la-Crosse of 1823 (p. 42) and the published Red River testimonies of 1818 (pp. 43–44). She presents women's studies as 'one important perspective, among several' (p. 40). Her presidential address to the American Society for Ethnohistory (Ethnohistory 38:2, 1991) is known through an indexed excerpt only, OpenAlex's abstract field; the page itself was not inspected. It speaks of 'the rather obscure niche occupied by our field, methodology, approach, or whatever it is we do when we do ethnohistory', and offers 'auto-ethnohistory' as 'a useful handle for some reflections about ethnohistory and ethnohistorians, myself included' (indexed excerpt; p. 113 is the recorded first page). Title-level: The Orders of the Dreamed (with Brightman, 1988), an edition of the trader George Nelson's 1823 account of Cree and Northern Ojibwa religion and myth, and Reading Beyond Words: Contexts for Native History (ed. with Vibert, 1996). Reception, read in full: Fiske (Atlantis 25:1, 2000) cites Brown and Vibert (1996) for the literary turn 'that subjects both oral and written narratives to textual analysis' (p. 13). McPherson (2000, n. 31) cites an essay in that volume as discursive analysis of a Red River trial. Gresko (1981) objected to the 'bits of anthropological theory' in Strangers in Blood (p. 113). Later readings, labelled. Brown (2012, read in the 2017 reprint) recalls that 'my courses and professors directed me towards broader issues of method and theory'. She also says she 'benefited from confronting the multiple problems around defining such categories as "marriage," "custom," and "society"' (pp. 191–92). The 2017 part introduction calls the pair 'I coming from anthropology and Sylvia from history' (p. 159). Her essay 'The Blind Men and the Elephant' (1990) is read only in its revised 2017 reprint, which cites a 2014 book. There she asks historians to 'start by deconstructing' the fur trade, and warns that subsuming northern Native history under 'the fur trade era' restricts it to 'certain rather specialized "Indian-White relations"' (pp. 63–65); the 1990 wording is unchecked. The edge claims a contribution to the field's documentary method, not that she shaped ethnohistory as a whole.

named_group_routes.relationship: Gender and race in the making of a would-be white settler colony: British Columbia, 1849–71, where colonization and immigration were meant to produce a white, respectable society among a majority of Aboriginal people and failed to do so (2001), which she said was inspired by an international literature on gender and colonialism (no derivation from Wolfe's settler-colonial theory is established by the texts checked); later described by her as a comparative settler-colonial argument (2016)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own words, in period. 'Presence, Absence, and the Writing of BC History', BC Studies 132 (2001/02), pp. 57–64, read in full: On the Edge of Empire 'was initially inspired not by local experience but by a rich international literature on gender and colonialism. That through reading about imperialism elsewhere I came to see imperialism where I was is a suggestive comment on the convenient erasure of dispossession' (p. 58; the sentence ends 'settler consciousness' without a connecting word); 'The most remarkable pattern of silence probably concerns Aboriginal peoples' (p. 61). The 1995 essay (pp. 42–43, read) calls British Columbia 'a racially divided one controlled by a minority white population constantly engaged in a process of colonization' (p. 42). The book is unread; reviewers quote it: 'In contemporary newspapers and conversations, White British Columbians often long for the days when our society was unquestionably British … When we do so we long for a fiction of our own invention' (p. 201, as quoted by Carter, p. 117). In-period reviews. Sarah Carter, BC Studies 136 (2002/03), pp. 117–119, read in full: 'British Columbia fits within a broader context of European colonialism in that it was a settler colony where dispossesion [sic] of the indigenous societies and resettlement by a newcomer population were intertwined. While this is imperial history, it is not an example of the triumph of imperialism as in this era Aboriginal peoples remained demographically dominant and socially central' (p. 117); but 'The theme of the "social centrality and political agency" of the Aboriginal peoples of British Columbia could have been further developed' (p. 119). Myra Rutherdale, Labour/Le Travail 50 (2002), pp. 324–326, read in full: Perry shows 'how colonization and immigration worked in tandem in an attempt to create a White colony, while at the same time deliberately marginalizing the majority of the population, the Aboriginal peoples' (p. 325). Paul Orlowski, Left History 8:1 (2002), pp. 119–122, read in full: 'I found Perry's rendering of First Nations resistance to be lacking throughout much of the work, their portrayal emphasizing passivity rather than agency' (p. 121). Her own caution (1995, p. 43): 'my analysis minimizes the subjectivity of First Nations people'. No derivation from Wolfe is established by the texts checked: the 2001 essay cites Said, McClintock, Burton and Chakrabarty, not Wolfe, and the book is unread; the settler_colonialism roster already says Perry wrote 'earlier or beside' the paradigm. Later readings, labelled: in the BC Studies 190 forum (2016) she says the 2001 book 'makes the argument that British Columbia's history is best understood within a comparative framework of settler colonialism, echoing an assumption that undergirds Cole Harris's 1997 and 2002 books' (p. 112); Tony Ballantyne (2016, pp. 104–105) reads Colonial Relations (2015) as 'a salutary reminder of the limitations of work that follows Patrick Wolfe and Lorenzo Veracini in understanding "settler colonialism" as a fundamentally eliminationist project'.
named_group_routes.map_label: Gender, race and a settler colony, 1995–2001

named_group_routes.relationship: Race in the history of white women and gender in the Canadian West: the 'scarcity model' and 'volcano theory' of gender imbalance traced to colonial promoters (1995), and white masculinity, mixed-race relationships and assisted female migration in colonial British Columbia read as the making of whiteness (2001)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own words, in period. '“Oh I’m Just Sick of the Faces of Men”', BC Studies 105/106 (1995), pp. 27–44, read at pp. 27–33 and 42–43: Canadian historians used 'the "scarcity model" (the notion that women's experience improves commensurately with their scarcity) and the "volcano theory" of male sexuality (the assumption of a fixed quantity of male sexual energy)' (p. 27); 'a quarter-century of inquiry into women's history has produced little on the effect of a skewed demography on women's experience' (p. 28); its 'most clear example' is Jan Noel's 'New France: Les femmes favorisées' (p. 29 n. 4); both models 'are based on essentialist understandings of both sexuality and race. Practitioners of the "scarcity model" never compute aboriginal women (or, for that matter, men) into their arithmetical evaluation' (p. 30); they are 'integral not only to twentieth century scholarship, but also to colonial discourse itself' (p. 31), descending from Wakefield and the colonial promoters (p. 32); white women's experience 'was never determined by gender alone. British Columbia was a class society' (p. 42); 'While gender imbalance increased white women's opportunities for heterosexual contact, it restricted those economic and social possibilities not contained within the heterosexual nexus' (p. 43). On the Edge of Empire (2001) is unread; Orlowski (p. 119) quotes its aim, 'the importance of race to the social experience of gender in nineteenth-century British Columbia' (p. 8), and 'a sharp disjuncture between colonial discourse and colonial practice on this edge of empire' (p. 167, quoted p. 120; Carter, p. 119, uses the same phrase). In-period reception, read in full: Carter (2002): 'This book also makes a valuable Canadian contribution to "Whiteness" studies' (p. 117); Rutherdale (2002): 'At the heart of this imagined community was Whiteness' (p. 325), and the reformers' hope that white women were the 'imperial panacea' (p. 4, as quoted p. 326). Critics: Orlowski (2002) holds that she 'fails to invoke what Roediger calls the "wages of whiteness"', leaving 'a binary racial divide that runs through the entire book but did not run through colonial British Columbia', with Chinese labourers set aside (p. 121), and that her claim that 'class relations are central to social relations' receives little attention (p. 121); Carter (p. 119) asks for the North American setting ('This edge of empire had much in common with California'); Rutherdale's 'small quibble' is that the 'Home' and 'Away' relationship 'could be further probed' (p. 326). Distinct from the Van Kirk packet's edges on fur-trade women: this edge is the post-fur-trade settler colony and the critique of the scarcity model.

named_group_routes.relationship: Mixed-race relationships not to be explained by white women's absence: Perry's 1995 criticism of fur-trade historians, Van Kirk's 'brilliant account' included, for treating intermarriage as the product of that absence, and her 2001 argument (as Carter reports it) that such relationships were 'not confined to the fur trade' and that 'happy stories' of fur-trade marriages can 'obscure both coercive details and the larger brutality of colonialism'
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own words, in period. 1995 (BC Studies 105/106, read at p. 30): 'Historians of the fur trade, while concerned with establishing the salience of mixed-race relationships, nonetheless explain their frequency as the product of white women's absence'; n. 8: 'For a brilliant account which ultimately suggests that the existence of mixed-race relationships was the result of white women's absence from the fur trade, see Sylvia Van Kirk, "Many Tender Ties" … Also see Jennifer S. H. Brown, Strangers in Blood … and Robin Fisher, Contact and Conflict'; n. 11 quotes Van Kirk: 'Had it been possible for fur traders to bring their wives out at an earlier date, it is doubtful whether intermarriage with native women would have been so extensive' (Many Tender Ties, p. 173); the 'volcano theory' 'holds that mixed-race relationships are at worst unfathomable and at best the products of abnormal historical circumstances' (p. 30). Qualifications kept: the criticism is of one explanation, not of the field; she calls Van Kirk's account 'brilliant' (p. 30 n. 8) and 'pioneering' (p. 43), and relies on it for the displacement of Aboriginal women (p. 43). 2001: the book is unread; Carter (BC Studies 136, p. 118, read) reports that 'Perry does not write a history of these relationships, noting the difficulties with available sources, but she does argue that they were not confined to the fur trade and could be found in the city, in the country, and in mining towns', and that she 'stresses the need to look beyond the "happy stories," such as the long marriage of James Douglas and Amelia Connolly, that can "obscure both coercive details and the larger brutality of colonialism" (62)'. In-period counterpoint: Orlowski (2002, p. 121, read) faults the book because 'the mixed-race couples in colonial B.C. had much to do with building alliances, sometimes between Hudson's Bay Company officers and the daughters of Aboriginal chiefs, a strategy that is not considered at all in the book'. No reply by Van Kirk or Brown was checked. Later reading, labelled: in 2016 (p. 113) she proposes thinking 'seriously about fur-trade colonialism as a distinct and meaningful practice of empire' (Colonial Relations, on the Douglas–Connolly family, is unread). Target: Van Kirk's person entry, since the criticism is of her explanation of intermarriage; her entry cites Perry's 2008 essay on her work only as a later reading.
named_group_routes.map_label: Perry: mixed-race unions beyond white women's absence, 1995–2001

named_group_routes.relationship: Feminist and postcolonial work on gender, race and colonial categories (Stoler and McClintock, as she and her reviewers name them, with Said and Burton) as the 'international literature on gender and colonialism' that she said inspired On the Edge of Empire (2001), used with a caution about analysing 'white discourse and white discourse alone' (1995)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own words. 2001 (BC Studies 132, p. 58, read): the book 'was initially inspired not by local experience but by a rich international literature on gender and colonialism'; 'Edward Said's Orientalism contains the germinal insight that such stock knowledge functioned to inform and serve the centre rather than to understand the various peripheries about which, putatively, it spoke' (pp. 58–59); Burton's argument, as Perry puts it, that knowledge of margins should 'unpack the intimate wedding of historical scholarship to the nation-state' (p. 59, citing Burton in Catherine Hall's Cultures of Empire reader); Anne McClintock's 'anachronistic space' (p. 61); Chakrabarty 'convincingly argues' that history cannot be disaggregated 'from the politics of Western supremacy that produced it' (pp. 63–64). 1995 (p. 43, read), on scholars of colonial discourse who 'analyse white discourse and white discourse alone': the position 'contains an important critique of the intellectual conceit' in historians' attempts to represent the colonized, but 'it can also function to legitimize the neglect of First Nations histories'. In-period reviewers, their characterisations: Rutherdale (Labour/Le Travail 50, 2002, p. 325, read): 'Influenced by the work of Anne Laura Stoler, Perry argues that because "white and Aboriginal people shared ties, homes, children, and labour," they "challenged colonialism's foundational fiction"' (p. 123 of the book), and the book is 'informed by an international post-colonial, feminist, gendered, and Marxist analysis'; Orlowski (Left History 8:1, 2002, pp. 119–120, read): she is 'positioned within feminist postcolonial scholars such as Ann Laura Stoler, Robert J. C. Young, and Anne McClintock, all of whom she refers to in the book', and she uses 'discourse' in 'the Foucauldian sense', though she 'never defines' it (p. 121). The book itself is unread, so the influence of Stoler rests on the reviewers' statements. Stoler, McClintock and Burton have no atlas entries; Stoler is on the post roster (colonial_intimacies) and the gender roster (colonial_categories), Said has a person entry.

named_group_routes.relationship: Practical realism with Joyce Appleby and Margaret Jacob (1994) and a reassessment of the cultural turn with Victoria Bonnell (1999)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Existing readings. Telling the Truth about History (appleby_hunt_jacob): all three authors share every chapter; the chapter 7 "Practical Realism" section and notes name Putnam and Peirce as resources; chapter 8: "It is time to come out of the trenches." Beyond the Cultural Turn (bonnell_hunt_primary): the editors' introduction (pp. 1, 12–25 read) presents competing reassessments and explicitly acknowledges White's disagreement in his afterword. A particular response within the debate, not its resolution; co-author credits retained.
named_group_routes.map_label: Practical realism and beyond the cultural turn, 1994–99

named_group_routes.relationship: Englishness as a formation of class, gender and race: imperial men, masculinities and “raced” white subjects (2002–2003)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own retrospective statement, read by the second research pass (JBS 42:4, 2003): her task was "to analyze the 'racing,' to use Toni Morrison's term, of white subjects, the ways in which Englishness needs to be understood not only as a formation of class and of gender, but also of race and ethnicity" (p. 531); the book "is about men, masculinities, and the making of 'raced' subjects" (p. 536); she concedes to Holt and Levine that "There is undoubtedly more that I could have done with the women" (pp. 536–537). Civilising Subjects itself is unread. Distinct from the 1987 Family Fortunes contribution, which reaches gender history through edge_757's social-history claim and the existing roster row.

named_group_routes.relationship: Four questions put to White (1993): whether a determinist theory of language fits the freedom White grants historians, whether his tropology should itself be historicised, what becomes of research's “heavy and demanding operations”, and how his relativism answers the Shoah and its deniers, as White restates them in his rejoinder
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Chartier's article ("Quatre questions à Hayden White", Storia della Storiografia 24, 1993, 133–142) is unread. The four questions are known through White's 1995 rejoinder, read in full in its authorised Portuguese translation (Revista de Teoria da História 28, 2025, published 14 April 2026): (1) whether it is "contraditório" to invoke a post-Saussurean, "determinista" theory of language while granting historians a poet's freedom (p. 4); (2) whether he treated one tropology as inherent to Western consciousness instead of contextualising the historians' discourses (p. 5); (3) how to regard "opérations très lourdes et exigeantes que sont la constitution d'un corpus documentaire, le contrôle des données et des hypothèses, la construction d'interprétation" (Chartier's French, quoted by White, p. 6); (4) how White's "relativismo" meets the demand for truth raised by the "crimes commis par les tyrannies ou, plus encore, la Shoah" and by revisionist denial (pp. 7–8). Metadata of both articles from Domańska's bibliography. White calls the exchange friendly (p. 4); a critique of Metahistory's assumptions, not a rejection of White's work as a whole.
named_group_routes.map_label: Chartier’s four questions to White, 1993, as White restates them

named_group_routes.relationship: White’s rejoinder (1995): no contradiction between linguistic codes that limit what can be said and freely chosen codes; his tropology was dominant in Western discourse from the late Renaissance; much of erudition’s apparatus is a ritual “theatre” of good faith; Holocaust denial raises no methodological question
named_group_routes.evidence_note: White's own words, read in full in the authorised Portuguese translation (Revista de Teoria da História 28, 2025, e83664, published 14 April 2026; English renderings are atlas translations from Portuguese; the 1995 English original, Storia della Storiografia 27, 63–70, not seen). "Eu estava falando de discursos, não do cosmos" (p. 4); the fourfold tropology was "culturalmente dominante no Ocidente desde o final do Renascimento até o Modernismo", and "O modelo talvez tenha sido menos útil do que eu imaginava; não foi muito bem recebido. Mas era melhor, penso eu, do que não ter modelo nenhum" (p. 5); "A tradução das coisas da realidade em coisas do discurso é uma ficcionalização" and much of the operations Chartier names "pertence ao “teatro” da erudição acadêmica; tem uma função ritual" (pp. 6–7); the deniers "simplesmente (e de forma bastante perversa) negam a ocorrência de certos eventos", and "Não há qualquer questão metodológica em jogo" (pp. 7–8). A reply within a courteous exchange (p. 4), including a concession about his model's reception.

named_group_routes.relationship: Practices are not reducible to discourse: the logic of discourses differs from the logic of conduct, social positions are conditions of possibility of discourse, and cultural historians have moved away from “the illusions of the linguistic turn” (2003)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own words, read in full (Cahiers du CRH 31, 2003, OpenEdition; paragraphs cited). The linguistic turn holds "que la « réalité » n'est pas une référence objective, extérieure au discours"; against it, accessing past practices through texts does not mean "affirmer l'identité de deux logiques" (¶25). Social positions "ne sont pas seulement un effet des discours ; elles en désignent également les conditions de possibilité" (¶26). Cultural historians "se sont éloignés tant des illusions du tournant linguistique que des héritages contraignants qui postulaient le primat du politique ou la toute-puissance du social" (¶31). Foucault's own distinction between discursive formations and non-discursive systems is one of his resources (¶25 n. 25), so this is a critique of a position, not of every author grouped under this entry; Hayden White is not named in the article.

named_group_routes.relationship: In Herman Paul’s 2019 assessment, White’s work became philosophy of history’s shared reference point, built on by Harlan, Kleinberg and Kuukkanen and contested by others; White himself assigned philosophy of history to the “practical past” (2010)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Paul's author manuscript, read in full (Journal of the Philosophy of History 13, 2019; manuscript pages): "no other author occupies a position in the field that is remotely as central as White’s" (ms 1); his only measure is his own JSTOR count of History and Theory articles mentioning White (ms 10 n. 22), with Harlan, Kleinberg and Kuukkanen positioning themselves towards him (ms 10–11). White's own words, read in full (Historein 10, 2010, p. 18): "philosophy of history belongs to the class of disciplines meant to bring order and reason to a 'practical past'". Counterweight: Timmins (Reviews in History, 2011) remains "to be convinced that White's impact on historical writing is as great as the current narratives claim" — a claim about historians' practice, not philosophy of history. Reciprocal to edge_166 (the earlier philosophers White engaged), not parallel to it.
named_group_routes.map_label: Paul: White as the field’s reference point, 2019

named_group_routes.relationship: Philosophers of history contest White’s narrativism, as Herman Paul reports: Ricoeur on the constraints set by sources, David Carr on narrative in lived experience, Lorenz’s internal realism, Ankersmit on untheorised tropes and Runia on presence (1985–2013)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Mediated: the critics' texts are unread and known through Paul's manuscript, read in full (2019, ms 17–19): Ankersmit finds the tropology "not nearly philosophical enough"; for Ricoeur sources "set constraints" and White "runs a risk of erasing genre boundaries between history and fiction" (Temps et récit 3, 1985); David Carr (1986); "'internal realists' such as Chris Lorenz argue that White downplays the importance of rational debate among historians"; Runia's "presence" against "Whitean representationalism" (2006). Paul's caveat: criticism is sometimes "a response elicited by the perceived dominance of his work" (ms 19). A second witness for David Carr: Cronon (1992, pp. 1368–1369, read) prefers Carr's position to White's and Mink's. Distinct from edge_257, where historians (Ginzburg, Evans) answer postmodernism.
named_group_routes.map_label: Ricoeur, David Carr, Lorenz, Ankersmit, Runia, per Paul

named_group_routes.relationship: A historian of European thought before Metahistory, who coauthored two textbooks on liberal humanism in Western Europe (1966, 1970) and wrote essays on the tasks of intellectual history, as Paul and Sanz Loroño report; Martin Jay ranks his reflections on the craft with Skinner’s (2013)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Mediated: the 1960s books and essays are unread. Paul (2019, ms 13 n. 32, read in full): The Emergence of Liberal Humanism: An Intellectual History of Western Europe (1966, with Coates and Schapiro) and The Ordeal of Liberal Humanism (1970, with Coates). Sanz Loroño (Historiografías, 2011, p. 143, read in full): The Fiction of Narrative reprints "The tasks of intellectual history" and "Romanticism, historicism, and realism", the latter readable "como un Metahistory anterior al impacto del (pos) estructuralismo francés". Stovall's AHA memorial (2018, WebFetch) presents him as an intellectual historian and theorist. Jay (History and Theory, 2013, abstract only): "No contemporary intellectual historian has produced more influential reflections on the historian's craft than Hayden White and Quentin Skinner". No strand is targeted.
named_group_routes.map_label: Intellectual historian of Europe, per readers

named_group_routes.relationship: White asks what limits govern the stories that can responsibly be told about the Holocaust (Probing the Limits of Representation, 1992; reprinted in Figural Realism); the quoted excerpt makes a conditional argument about facts determining plots. His 2014 contents also list “Truth and Circumstance …”; that chapter is unread
named_group_routes.evidence_note: An excerpt witness: the passages of the essay quoted by Claus and Marriott, whose framing is theirs (white_emplotment_excerpt, existing reading, re-read for revision 1.147): "Are there any limits on the kind of story that can responsibly be told about these phenomena?"; facts set limits on stories "only if we believe that the events themselves possess a 'story' kind of form and a 'plot' kind of meaning" — a conditional argument about facts determining plots, not a claim that all emplotments are equally valid, and not the full argument of the chapter. The essay's pages (37–53 in Friedländer's volume) and its discussion by Ginzburg and Funkenstein come from Domańska's bibliography; MUSE contents show it reprinted as Figural Realism ch. 2 (pp. 27–42) and the 2014 chapter "Truth and Circumstance: What (if Anything) Can Properly Be Said about the Holocaust?" (pp. 25–40), both unread. Paul (2019, ms 15) records his later "forays into 'modernist events,' … witness literature, trauma". Holocaust representation was previously carried only at group level (edges 223, 224) and in Friedländer's roster row.

named_group_routes.relationship: Cronon builds on White’s distinction between chronicle and narrative, then sides with David Carr against the White–Mink view that historians impose plots on reality (1992)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Cronon's own text, read in part for this edge ("A Place for Stories", JAH 78:4, 1992, author-hosted copy in journal pagination): p. 1351 n. 7, "This distinction between chronicle and narrative is more fully analyzed in White, Metahistory, 5-7; White, Tropics of Discourse, 109-11"; p. 1368, White and Mink "argue that narrative is so basic to our cultural beliefs that we automatically impose it on a reality that bears little or no relation to the plots we use" (Cronon's summary of their position); n. 39 calls White's 1984 survey "useful, if biased"; pp. 1368–1369, Carr's position "gives us a way of absorbing the lessons of narrative theory without feeling we have abandoned all ties to an external reality". One essay makes both moves, so one arrow records an acknowledged and contested resource (the pattern of edge_646). edge_903 (Cronon → truthdebate) uses other pages of the same essay for his own position.
named_group_routes.map_label: Chronicle and narrative: used and contested, 1992

named_group_routes.relationship: 'A global history of Britain … not because of that old imperial conceit that Britain made the world, but because the world made Britain' (2016; Modern Britain, 2017); against 'Britain and the world' as a field that can 'reanimate an Anglo world in which white men invariably occupy center stage' (2018); neoliberalism seen from Heathrow (2021)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own words: History Australia abstract (2016, read): 'I propose a global history of modern Britain around an account of the rise, demise and reinvention of a liberal political economy … This history of Britain is then a global story, not because of that old imperial conceit that Britain made the world, but because the world made Britain.' JBS 2018 forum (his section read): an imperial history of the British world can 'reanimate an Anglo world in which white men invariably occupy center stage'; 'a global history of Britain concerned with how the world made Britain'. Heathrow abstract (2021, read): neoliberalism 'less about the global flow of ideas and capital than the local social formations and labour regimes engendered by changing forms of accumulation'. Cambridge descriptions of Modern Britain (2017; 2025).

named_group_routes.relationship: Perry named Stoler (with McClintock, Said and Burton) in the 'international literature on gender and colonialism' that inspired On the Edge of Empire (2001), with a caution about analysing 'white discourse and white discourse alone' (1995); Perry later wrote 'The Colonial Archive on Trial' in Burton's Archive Stories (2005)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Rests on the evidence already recorded for edge_1023 (post → adele_perry): Perry's own 2001 statement and her 1995 caution, read in an earlier revision (pe139_perry_presence_2001, pe139_perry_sick_1995); Burton's contents (Duke page, read). The person-level arrow makes the influence that edge_1023 attributes to a field attributable to its named author; edge_1023 itself is unchanged. Perry's chapter is unread.

named_group_routes.relationship: Settler colonialism against underdevelopment: the 1970s–80s 'settler/dominion capitalism' literature made the settler colony 'the opposite of colonialism and associated underdevelopment' (Veracini 2013 on Denoon 1983); Englert returns the question through Harvey's accumulation by dispossession (2020)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Veracini 2013 (abstract, existing record; author manuscript read): in the third phase "settler colonialism is understood as the opposite of colonialism and associated underdevelopment and political fragmentation", and the settler-capitalism approach wrote "indigenous people and indigenous history off the conceptual map". Denoon 1983 at title level (existing). Englert 2020 (read in full): accumulation by dispossession "as developed by David Harvey (2003)" proposed as the alternative to the elimination model, with Emmanuel's 1972 NLR essay on white-settler colonialism in his bibliography. A comparison of frames; no descent asserted. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

named_group_routes.relationship: Black Women in White (1989) studies Black nurses’ struggles against racial and gender exclusion; Hine’s later argument makes parallel professional organizations important to resistance (2003).
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The nursing-book interpretation is attributed to Celia J. Wintz’s read repository abstract; the book is not newly read. Hine’s 2003 published opening extract, rather than the whole address, supplies the parallel-institutions argument. A scoped contribution to nursing/professional history, not founding medical history.

named_group_routes.relationship: With Deborah Gray White and a collective of researchers, Scarlet and Black (2016) brings Rutgers’s involvement in slavery and dispossession into the university’s public history.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Publisher description and contents, read, establish a jointly edited committee publication with separately named chapter authors. White wrote its introduction; Fuentes is neither sole author nor sole discoverer. Contribution is scoped to this collaborative publication and stated public purpose, not a general claim to founding public history.

named_group_routes.relationship: Investigates how claims about civilization could authorize white male power or be turned against it.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Primary chapter-1 closing passage on four distinct cases, indexed printed pp. 42–43. The prose on historical actors is Bederman’s argument, not an endorsement of their racial categories. No claim that the entire book or its cited archival evidence was independently read.

named_group_routes.relationship: Examines white-worker identity as historically constructed and as a constraint on class solidarity.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own interview distinguishes historical racialization from natural race and explicitly denies race explains everything about labour conservatism.

named_group_routes.relationship: Self-Rule interprets American democracy through participatory institutions and the constraints of centralization and hierarchy.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Ashley Woodiwiss1996 reading; earlier white-male democracy’s exclusions remain explicit rather than an idealized universal democracy.

named_group_routes.relationship: Shows Prohibition enforcement becoming an instrument of white Protestant supremacy and unequal coercion.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own Herrin answer identifies Klan recruitment and selective action against ethnic/religious targets; one locality is not presented as every locality.

named_group_routes.relationship: Deloria criticizes Turner’s frontier boundary for naturalizing Indigenous difference and an expectation of inevitable white triumph (2002).
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Primary publisher excerpt 8–10, with 6–7 framing. Deloria situates Turner within a longer frontier paradigm; this neither makes Turner its sole inventor nor treats all Indigenous historiography as one position. Remaining chapter unread.
